item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Harpies, nagas, and sphinxes1 all fit as girl monsters.
Female minotaurs and centaurs are a bit off-model, just not enough to distract me while reading.
But lady satyrs really jam a wrench in my mental gears.

The traditional mythology holds that half-goats are definitively, emphatically, elementally male; and I can't conceive of any process that would spin that legend out of this "factual" seed of all-female hybrids.
A better fit for the theme would be a cetacean hybrid.
Even if it's only me bugged by fem-satyrs (and it probably only is), leaving out mermaids is missing a trick.

That being said, I like this version a lot more than the original seductress-voiced one with the ham-fisted cross-linking.

Footnotes
1. Or is the plural "sphinx"?

item.content:encoded:
I know. However, all the other haplotypes produce random animals, and the Old Testament tends to get rather nasty towards non-Hebrew people being sub-human. Nothing in the article seemed to imply that this process is unnatural—-as in, the implications for some SCPs dealing with real mythology tend towards a realistic explanation of the myth, or a confirmation on a certain level, rather than it being the mentality of the SCP or the researchers themselves. This article seems to be written along the same lines.

Best example I can come up with: in "I Am Legend" (book), the vampires are "repelled" by crucifixes not because of any inherent truth or power in the symbol or in Christianity, but because of the vampire's own psychological mindset and/or set of beliefs. By such logic, Jewish vampires would be repelled by the Star of David, and so on.

The way I interpreted this article makes it seem like the "crucifixes" have an inherent truth or power in their own right when mixed with the SCP, rather than it being a bias or preference shown by the SCP

On its own, this is an interesting SCP. The thing that confuses me the most is the earlier posts on this discussion page expressing dislike for 336 just because of the sort-of-Biblical reference. I mean, I'm not a particular fan of Christianity - on the contrary, I [REDACTED] - but some of my favorite SCP's and Tales (like 076, and Incident 239-B and the subsequent interview with Dr. Clef) have Biblical roots. I'm not protesting, per se, I'm just confused.
Personally, I would love to see someone combine the old and new versions of this SCP. For instance, put her name back into the actual article, as well as her origins, without removing anything for the sake of it; keep the scales on her legs, but give her back the wing stubs; and, most of all, keep the new effects of her voice on people, but give back her hypnotic power - I mean, as it stands right now, people exposed to her voice get these weird symptoms, but her words have no effect on anything, so people can just talk with her normally and only later discover that something weird happened to them, which seems kind of…silly, for lack of a better word. Just a thought.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There's a reason we specifically phrased it as "Subjects lacking a Y chromosome and possessing otherwise healthy reproductive systems" and "Subjects with a Y chromosome". Anyone with a Y is going to get a chimera. Anyone without a Y is going to get sterility, but since a subject missing an X or suffering from trisomy X is rather unlikely to be able to reproduce viably, it's of little consequence.

As an aside: I was aware of these possibilities in the genetic aspect, but I don't think I recall anything about XX genotypes being able to produce male sex organs. It's moot with regards to the article, but it has me academically curious.

item.content:encoded:
Not sure about the female infertility, but as for the rest: Lilith was supposedly formed in the same way that Adam was, rather than Eve, who came from Adam's rib (see also why they specifically mention that the critters come from extra bits such as ribs). As for the critters themselves, there are some mythological tales (not sure how old they are), that say that Lilith was the mother of many monsters, having mated with demons after being expelled from Eden. This myth appears to be a conflation of the Greek myth of Echnida, who was called the Mother of Monsters, and birthed a wide variety of monsters of many types. As I recall, she was the mother of Scylla and/or Charybdis, for instance.

Anyhoo, I like this version.

Ok. Scantron and I have completed the rewrite. Since the abilities of the original Lilith weren't all that interesting, we went back to the original mythology for a base. What one quickly realizes is that the existing mythology for Lilith is an atrocious mess of maybe-this-maybe-that, some of it from ancient times and some of it from no more than a few hundred years ago.

What we have here pulls a few scraps from some of the older myths, one or two from the newer ones, and blends in a figure from Greek myth too for good measure. Let us know what you think.
